(ORAL)
1. Vide this order, I propose to dispose of the present Criminal Appeal filed against the order of conviction dated 30.11.2015 and order of sentence dated 07.12.2015 passed by Ld. ACMM-II, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi.
2. I have heard the arguments in the present case.
Satish Kumar vs Department Of P.F.A on 22 November, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/47982367/
1

3. The brief allegations in the present case are that the officials from the Department had heard about synthetic milk being sold in the trans-Yamuna area and accordingly, they raided M/s Deepak Milk Centre at Naveen Shahdra, Delhi at around 06:00 PM on 22.12.1999.
4.

When they disclosed their identity and purpose of visiting the said shop, the milk stored in the stainless steel jar was thrown on the ground by an employee Satish Kumar at the instance of Deepak Kumar, the proprietor of the shop.
5. Immediately, a sample of the spilled milk was taken by the Food Inspector and the stainless steel container was also seized.
Police was called and ultimately an FIR also came to be registered under Section 186/353/34 IPC for preventing the Food Inspector from performing his duty and taking a sample.
6. The sample so lifted from the ground was never sent to the PA for examination.

However, one more sample of milk was lifted from another drum lying in the shop and that sample conforms to the standards laid down and, therefore, prosecution in the present case was lodged only u/s 16(1)(c)
and (d) of PFA as a complaint case and a charge-sheet was filed for offence u/s 186/353/34 of IPC on the FIR.
Ultimately, both cases were clubbed and tried together and a common judgment passed.

7. Although, I have noticed that there are several contradictions in the testimony of the witnesses viz-a-viz the place where the drum was lying at the time when the sample was proposed to be taken,
as also, viz-a-viz who had thrown the milk and the manner in which the milk was lifted from the ground and placed in the bottle, however, it needs to be seen that witnesses in the present case were examined 10 years after the alleged incident and over the passage of time minor contradictions are bound to arise in the testimony of the witnesses.

8. Further, there is no complaint placed on record on behalf of the accused persons that a false case was registered against them on the pretext that they had thrown the milk, whereas in the evidence, it was being suggested to the witnesses that when the milk vendor tried to lift the Can/drum from the premises, he was stopped by the PFA Staff and in the said process the said utensil had fallen on the ground.

Further, the accused persons had neither appeared as defence witnesses and examined themselves to depose that the milk had fallen due to an accident and not intentionally spilled nor the said alleged milk vendor was produced as a defence witness, although, only a suggestion was given to PW-3 in this regard.
In any event, the same implies that milk was in fact spilled on that day.

9. Further, I may note that even this suggestion was not given to all the witnesses but only to PW-3 and, therefore, even this defence was not uniformly without variance put to all the witnesses of the process of sampling.

10. In my view, the accused was bound to put this defence and version of how the milk spilled to all the witnesses of process of taking of sample and merely it was put to PW-3, it would not come to the aid of the accused persons.

sentences.text: How the sample of the milk was lifted from the floor is not relevant inasmuch as the same was never sent to laboratory for testing and it would not make any difference as to how the sample was collected as compliance of Rule 14 on this sample is not called for nor required to be examined.
Therefore, I am of the view that the prosecution has been able to establish its case against the accused.

However, unfortunately, the milk which was lifted was never sent for testing and it could not be known whether the said milk was adulterated or not and the other sample lifted from the shop of the accused was found to be in order and not adulterated and, therefore, I am not in a position to conclude one way or other as to the reason for the accused to spill the milk.
It is possible that the same was done in the heat of movement on an argument taking place with the staff/officials who had come to collect the sample.
Therefore, I am of the view that the appeal against the order of conviction must fail on this count.
12. Be that as it may.
At least adulteration against the accused has not been established.

However, in my view, the Trial Court failed to note Section 26 of the General Clauses Act which reads as follows:
"Provision as to offences punishable under two or more enactments.-Where an act or omission constitutes an offence under two or more enactments, then the offender shall be liable to be prosecuted and punished under either or any of those enactments, but shall not be liable to be punished twice for the same offence."

13. In the present case, the same act of the convict, i.e., throwing of milk for preventing/lifting of sample while arguing with the public servant and pushing him, would be covered both u/s 16 (1)(c)
and (d) of PFA Act and Section 186/353/34 of IPC.
14.
Simply speaking, there are two enactments dealing with the same situation as far as Food Inspector as public servant is concerned is concerned.

Therefore, if Section 26 of the General Clauses Act was applicable, the accused could have been punished for only "either" or "any of the said enactment" and not under the both as has been done in the present case.

15. In fact, a complaint case and a police case under different enactments were filed and the accused was prosecuted under both and ultimately resulting in his conviction under both the enactments for the same Act.
16. Therefore, clearly there is an error in the judgment of the Trial Court.
The only reason this error was not apparent and hurting the convict was because the sentences were directed to run concurrently.

In case the sentences had been directed to run consecutively, the effect would have been more prominent and easily noticeable and the same would have clearly violated the constitutional right of the accused against double jeopardy or being punished twice for the same act which may constitute an offence under two enactments.
That is the very purpose of having Section 26 of General Clauses Act, which is slightly different from the provision contained in Section 71 of IPC.
In that view of the matter, the order on conviction and sentence call for interference.
17. Therefore, the conviction of the accused is reduced to one under Section 16(1)(c) and (d) of PFA Act, the same being a special statute.
That takes me to the order on sentence.

sentences.text: It is further noteworthy that more than 23 years have elapsed since the incident took place.
The accused Deepak is now 43 years old and, therefore, at the time when the offence was committed, he was only 20 years old and would have definitely qualified as a young offender.
19. As far as accused Satish Kumar is concerned.

Accused Satish Kumar has submitted that he is 42 years old as on date and, therefore, on the date of incident he was only 19 years old and as in case of accused Deepak Kumar, he was also within the age of (18-21) years and, therefore, would have fallen u/s 360 of Probation of Offenders Act.
20. I have further noticed that the age of the convicts as on the date of incident has not been noted nor considered by the Trial Court in the order on sentence.
In fact, it makes no reference whatsoever to the status of the convict on the date when the offence was committed and only deals with the situation as on the date of conviction.
The same is against settled Judicial Principle as well as the provision contained u/s 360 of Cr.P.C. which deals with young offenders below the age of 21 years.

I have also seen that no reasons have been given by the Trial Court as to why the provisions of Section 360 of Cr.P.C. or Probation of Offenders Act are not applicable or attracted to the facts and circumstances of the present case, which in my view, is another error in approach in dealing with the convict at the stage of passing of order on sentence.

I have also noticed that the order on sentence categorically records that the convict Deepak Kumar. was married and having a child who was only one year old on the date when the order on sentence was passed.
Further, no other involvement or conviction had been reported against the accused Deepak Kumar or Satish Kumar.

21. Further, I may note that in the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 which has replaced the PFA Act, deals with the offence of obstruction in Section 62 of the Act and provides for a punishment of imprisonment which may extend to three months and fine which may extend to Rs.1,00,000/-.
Therefore, the legislature has in its wisdom; reduced the rigour of the said offence.

22. I may further note that as far as the new Act is concerned, it has completely changed the regime as far as the food articles and its classification is concerned as well as what is adulteration but the offence of obstruction has been retained with lesser sentence.

23. However, having gone through the material and considering the fact that a minimum sentence was provided at least under the provisions of the PFA and considering that they were young offenders and 23 years have elapsed since the alleged offence took place and no subsequent conviction against them has been proved by the prosecution, their sentence is reduced to the payment of fine of Rs.20,000/- each for the offence u/s 16(1)
(c) and (d) of PFA Act and in default, SI for 15 days and substantive sentence of imprisonment till the rising of the Court.
Fine be deposited with the Trial Court, if not already deposited.
Convicts are given one week time to deposit the fine.
24. TRC to be undergone today itself.
25. Nothing survives in the present matter.
